attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'might' concession on per-token prices. The causal chain after it (more tokens, higher inference cost, bigger losses, more VC burn) is stated firmly, so treating it as a causal claim is right.

contract.note: Reading token growth as outweighing price cuts on comparable work is the ordinary reading of his firm causal language. Requiring matched-workload and financial evidence is demanding but fair, given how sweeping the chain is.

evidence.note: Anthropic's Nov 2025 disclosure says Opus 4.5 uses fewer tokens. It is the company's own claim and does not measure workload-weighted spending or losses.
OpenAI's Nov 2025 disclosure says GPT-5.1 uses fewer tokens on simple tasks and keeps reasoning longer on hard ones. It is company material and says the effect depends on workload.
A June 2025 preprint finds that verbose reasoning raises token cost. That backs the mechanism only. It does not trace costs to company losses or VC burn.

reviews.rationale: The packet has company claims of token efficiency and a preprint on how verbose reasoning raises costs. Nothing measures workload-weighted cost changes or traces token use to losses and VC consumption for these companies. The causal chain is neither established nor refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A close paraphrase. It drops 'massive' and 'becoming' and changes 'participating in' to 'redistributing', but the substance is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'drains' and 'redistribution of capital reserved for startups' as displacing other startups' funding is a fair, ordinary reading. Keeping commitments separate from realized payments is appropriate.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure of its $13B Series F (Sep 2025). It shows a large raise, but not where the money went or any displacement.
Anthropic's Nov 2025 disclosure shows it depends on cloud suppliers. It does not show how much capital was transferred.
CoreWeave's disclosure gives the total value of its OpenAI contract. That is a commitment, not cash paid in 2025.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows large raises and large supplier commitments. It does not show realized payments funded by investment capital, and nothing measures whether other startups lost funding as a result. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I believe' is not one of the hedges the policy lists, and the 'none will' exit claim is categorical, so it is a scorable forecast. The financial premises are present-tense and are left ungraded.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to AI-focused startups is a fair, narrower reading of 'every AI company'. One completed acquisition or IPO disproves 'none'. The financial premises are reasonably set aside.

evidence.note: Cursor's dated announcement (Aug 14, 2026) says its acquisition by SpaceX is complete. Cursor is an AI startup named in the post. This is a company disclosure, but it is the kind of closing record the contract prefers.

reviews.rationale: The exit forecast says no AI company will be acquired or go public. A completed acquisition of an AI startup after the post and before the evaluation date meets the contract's early-resolution rule and disproves it. The profitability and margin premises are not graded.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The profitability part is hedged ('may') and correctly kept as hedged. The firm part is 'will decline', a forecast of falling aggregate GPU rental prices with a stated cause and no deadline.

contract.note: An aggregate, like-for-like price measure is the ordinary reading. Requiring the supply mechanism is fair because he stated the cause. With no deadline, a finite stretch of rising prices cannot falsify the forecast.

evidence.note: Silicon Data's B200 neocloud index rose in 2026 (up 27.6% year to date, up 3.7% over three months). That cuts against the forecast so far, but it covers one GPU segment and a finite period, not the aggregate market.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The only evidence is one segment's price index, which rose rather than fell. That is unfavourable, but it does not settle an open-ended forecast about aggregate prices, and no event meets the early-resolution rule.
